answer_text:
Looking at this integral, I need to identify the structure of the integrand:

$$f(x) = \prod_{k=1}^{2002} \cos^k(kx)$$

## Step 1: Establish the Anti-Periodicity of $f(x)$

I'll check what happens when I shift $x$ by $\pi$:

$$\cos(k(x+\pi)) = \cos(kx + k\pi) = (-1)^k\cos(kx)$$

Therefore:

$$\cos^k(k(x+\pi)) = \left[(-1)^k \cos(kx)\right]^k = (-1)^{k^2}\cos^k(kx)$$

Multiplying over all $k = 1, \ldots, 2002$:

$$f(x+\pi) = (-1)^{\sum_{k=1}^{2002} k^2} \cdot f(x)$$

## Step 2: Determine the Parity of $\sum k^2$

Since $k^2 \equiv k \pmod{2}$:

$$\sum_{k=1}^{2002} k^2 \equiv \sum_{k=1}^{2002} k = \frac{2002 \cdot 2003}{2} = 1001 \times 2003 \pmod{2}$$

Both 1001 and 2003 are **odd**, so their product is **odd**.

## Step 3: Conclude the Anti-Periodicity

$$\boxed{f(x+\pi) = -f(x)}$$

This means $f$ has **period $2\pi$** and satisfies the anti-periodicity condition.

## Step 4: Evaluate the Integral

Split any full period $[0, 2\pi]$ into two halves:

$$\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{\pi} f(x)\,dx + \int_{\pi}^{2\pi} f(x)\,dx$$

In the second integral, substitute $x = t + \pi$:

$$\int_{\pi}^{2\pi} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{\pi} f(t+\pi)\,dt = \int_0^{\pi} (-f(t))\,dt = -\int_0^{\pi} f(t)\,dt$$

Therefore:

$$\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{\pi} f(t)\,dt + \left(-\int_0^{\pi} f(t)\,dt\right) = 0$$

The same logic applies to any interval of length $2\pi$, and by the additional symmetry $f(\pi - x) = -f(x)$ (verified similarly), the integral over $[0,\pi]$ also vanishes.

## Result

$$\int \cos x \cdot \cos^2(2x) \cdot \cos^3(3x) \cdots \cos^{2002}(2002x)\,dx = \boxed{0}$$

27B·v4.method: Uses anti-periodicity f(x+π)=-f(x) to split the integral over [0,2π] into two cancelling halves, yielding 0.
